After orders arrive in the system, each order will be assigned to the pod, each  pod  can  contain  multiple  orders.  In  this  study,  there  are  three different scenarios to conduct the order to pod assignment, including first come first  served  (FCFS),  order  batching  assignment,  and  two-phase assignment.  The  detailed  scenario  description  will  be  explained  in Section 3.2.1.
-  Pod sequencing
After the pod is assigned to the order, a list of selected pods will be sorted according  to  the  earliest  due  date  of  the  order.  The  sequence  of  the selected pod indicates the pod priorities to be picked.
-  Robot to Pod assignment
AGVs will be assigned to the selected pods based on the nearest distance and earliest due date. Take twice the number of available AGVs from the list of selected pods and the assignment is conducted between AGVs and the selected pods. However, the distance between AGV and the selected pod is calculated by Manhattan distance, and applying the Hungarian algorithm to obtain the assignment results
-  Robot routing

The routing policy of AGV applies Simple Routing with traffic control policy, which follows the previous study [47]. The traffic policy used is deadlock  and  collision  prevention.  This  simple  rule  in  AGV  routing enables it to have a minimum path without doing path planning, which can reduce the computational time for calculation.
- 
- Robot to workstation assignment (picking/ replenishment station)
When the robot reaches the highway in the storage area before going to the workstation, the assignment between robot and workstation is based on the minimum number of AGVs that queuing to be processed.
-  Robot to storage assignment
After finishing the picking or replenishment, the robot needs to bring the pod back to the storage area. The system will comprehensively consider all the AGVs that need to go to the empty locations in the storage area and all the empty positions together, then apply the Hungarian algorithm to determine the nearest empty location from the workstation.

After the pod finishes the order picking process, it will check the pod inventory level. If the inventory level lower than the certain percentage, the  pod  needs  to  be  replenished,  AGV  will  directly  bring  pod  to  the replenishment station.

Instead  of  assigning  the  order  to  the  picking  stations,  each  order  will  be assigned  to  a  pod.  Different  from  the  previous  related  work,  orders  would  be assigned to the picking station first, and then the required pod will be called to fulfill the order. However, it seems to be inefficient and will cause some restrictions if a picking station can only open up to three or six bins to place the ordered items, and when  the  orders  need  to  be  assigned  to  the  picking  stations,  it  will  have  the limitation of the number of bins for the order assignment. Instead of doing that, considering the flexibility of system resources [43], assuming the picking station can  handle  any  order,  the  assignment  between  orders  to  the  picking  station  is omitted, and the direct assignment for orders to pods can increase the possibility to optimize the order picking process. In this section, the scenarios of order-to-pod assignment and the formulation of optimization problem are illustrated in detail.

There are three scenarios for order-to-pod assignment: first come first served (FCFS) assignment, order batching assignment,  and two-phase  assignment.  The detailed descriptions are as follows.
First of all, FCFS assignment is a baseline for comparing with the other two scenarios, which is an assignment that handles order one by order. The flow chart of the FCFS assignment is shown in Figure 3.2.
After the order arrives, it will be assigned to the pod immediately. The FCFS assignment is based on the earliest due date rule, which means that the order will be assigned to the pod with the earliest due date. When it comes to multiple same options, it will be assigned to the pod randomly.
Figure 3.2 FCFS assignment flow chart

<!-- image -->
The second scenario is the order batching assignment, this scenario processes a number of orders in every assignment instead of handling orders one by one. The number of orders to be handled at once has a crucial role to increase pile-one value and in an attempt to reduce the number of picked pods as well. The flow chart of this scenario is shown in Figure 3.3.

The customer orders will arrive continuously, they will stay in the system and wait to be processed. After a certain number of orders arrive, they will be sorted by their  due  dates.  The  batch  size  will  be  determined,  and  the  corresponded  order batches  will  be  created  in  order.  Each  order  batch  as  a  group  of  orders  will  be assigned  at  once  in  an  assignment.  The  system  will  search  for  the  pods  which contain the same items as the orders in batches and its quantity is enough for the order, which means the qualified pods. The orders will be assigned to the qualified pods, and the optimization of the assignment is to assign them to pods with the minimum number. The formulation of optimization is described in the next section.
As for the batch size, since a large batch size will result in a lower throughput [28], it won't have too many orders in one batch. The next step of order to pod assignment is the robot to pod assignment, and the number of pods that could be assigned would be restricted by the number of the available robots, so if the number of orders in one batch is fixed in the first place, it could avoid the pod may not be allowed to be assigned to robots.

Figure 3.3 Order batching assignment flow chart

<!-- image -->
The third scenario is the proposed two-phase assignment. Same as the order batching assignment, this assignment handles a group of orders at once. The main difference  between  order  batching  assignment  and  two-phase  assignment  is  the system will identify the pod status and release parts of orders to the pods which have already been assigned to other orders before doing the order batching. The flow chart of the two-phase assignment is shown in Figure 3.4.
Figure 3.4 Two-phase assignment flow chart

<!-- image -->
In  order  to  identify  the  status  of  pods,  the  system  will  differentiate  the availability of pods in different steps. The status of pods is classified based on it is available to be assigned or not, and it could be divided into 6 different statuses, including:
-  Assigned pod
- -Static pod: waiting to be picked by robot

- -En-route pod: from storage area to the picking station
- -Queueing pod: waiting in the queue
- -Picking pod: picked by picker at the picking station
-  Unassigned pod
- -Idle pod: no assignment yet
- -Returning pod: after being picked, on the way back to the storage area

The pod will have different statuses in the moving processes. When the pod is in the storage area and hasn't been assigned to any order, at this point it is in an 'idle pod' status. After it is assigned to orders, the status will be turned into 'assigned pod' and wait to be picked by a robot, so it is classified as 'static pod'. When the robot arrives and picks the pod, it will be brought to the picking station from the storage area, and the status will be 'en-route pod'. After the pod reaches the picking station, it may need to wait for other pods to be processed in the queue, so the status is 'queueing pod'. When the pod is picked by the picker in the picking station, the status will change into 'picking pod' and not allow to be assigned anymore at this point. After the pod is done in the picking station, the robot will bring it back to the empty location of the storage area, and the status will be 'returning pod'. And the pod will be idle again after it is put back in the storage area. The cycle of the pod status is shown in Figure 3.5.

As for the overall process of the two-phase assignment scenario, after the order arrival and sorting. As shown in Figure 3.4, in Phase 1, the system will first identify the pod status and search for the assigned pods. If there are some orders that match the assigned pods, they will be assigned to those pods. In Phase 2, after releasing orders to the assigned pods, if there are some orders left, they will only be assigned to the unassigned pods, which are those still idle in the storage area or on the way for returning to the empty location.

RMFS is a parts-to-picker system that improves the picking rate significantly compared to the traditional methods especially for large e-commerce warehouses with many SKUs. It is critical for optimizing picking order, i.e. to collect more order items with less effort. Grouping multiple customer orders has been proven to be pivotal for an efficient way in the picking operation, with fulfilling more orders with less number of robots, which infer to less number of picked pods. The previous related research is choosing a pick order for the picking station. In contrast, this study assigns orders to pods. In this study, in order to fulfill more orders with fewer pods and increase the pile-on value at the same time, the order batching method is implemented in the order-to-pod assignment, handling orders in a group at once instead of one by one. Furthermore, the proposed two-phase assignment is divided into two steps to assign orders to pods, which first assign parts of orders to the pods that have been assigned to other orders, and then assign the rest of orders to the pods that haven't been assigned to any order in the second step.
The optimization objective is to minimize the number of picked pods while increasing the pile-on value as well.

This study conducts three simulations with different scenarios, including the FCFS  as  a  baseline,  order  batching  assignment,  and  the  proposed  two-phase assignment  for  order-to-pod  assignment.  By  implementing  the  order  batching method  for  order-to-pod  assignment,  it  can  significantly  reduce  the  number  of picked pods by 12.64% compared to the baseline simulation, and increase the pile- on value to 5.28. Moreover, the proposed two-phase assignment also includes order batching that can reduce more number of picked pods, which can reduce by 18.97% compared to the baseline, indicating that it only uses nearly half of the total number of pods. The pile-on value has also been increased significantly from the baseline of 2.87 to 6.37 in the two-phase assignment, which means around 6 order items be picked from one pod if applying two-phase assignment. Furthermore, order batch size may influence the throughput rate, however, in the two-phase assignment, the throughput efficiency doesn't drop too much, and it even reaches 98.11% when the batch size is 20. Noted that the batch size could not exceed the number of available robots, for avoiding the decrease of throughput. The  proposed

two-phase assignment process detects the pod status before the assignment, and then obtains better performance with higher pile-on value and fewer number of picked pods, which can reduce the robot movement and energy consumption.

In future work, the multi-line order can be considered in the order batching strategy for optimizing the order picking process. When there are multiple SKUs and different  quantities  of  order  items,  develop  a  different  method  to  deal  with orders for adapting the complexity is necessary. For the simulation, the charging process  of  AGVs  could  be  developed.  The  factors  of  AGV  movement  such  as acceleration, deceleration, and turning time can also be invested for deeper analysis. At the strategic level of RMFS, the warehouse layout including lots of elements, such as the number of workstations and their placement, pod batch size, and other configurations, that can be adjusted and find an optimal setting.
